80544.subject: 📉 Crypto crash continues
80544.body:
———————————————————————————

## Top Stories

**BTC** $83,093 (0.8%) | **ETH** $2,500 (-1.4%) | **SOL** $111 (-2.2%)

* Bitcoin falls below [$81,000](https://www.chooserich.live/story/bitcoin-falls-long-liquidations-surge-vv5ebn3), a 17-day low, as $100B leaves crypto market cap — Bitcoin spot ETFs post [$244M in outflows](https://www.chooserich.live/story/spot-bitcoin-etf-outflows-4xu55qj)

* Dow futures fall nearly 500 points as oil surges over 5%, yields hit [24-year highs](https://x.com/KobeissiLetter/status/2108160767031984207)

* OpenAI tells investors annualized revenue is nearing [$50B](https://www.chooserich.live/story/openai-annualized-revenue-expectations-e9mexhw), r==oughly $20 billion below expectations==

* SpaceX says Starlink will become a major[ US mobile carrier](https://x.com/WatcherGuru/status/2108293112732819773) — AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile each[ crater over 7%](https://x.com/KobeissiLetter/status/2108297720855241214)

* The US government moves over $1B of Bitcoin seized in the Bitfinex hack to an unknown wallet

* Jury convicts cybersecurity consultant over [$55M](https://www.chooserich.live/story/uranium-finance-crypto-theft-conviction-dssuivf) Uranium Finance theft including a $500K MTG Black Lotus

* Samsung Wallet adds native USDC support for [82M](https://www.chooserich.live/story/samsung-solana-usdc-transfers-u8jverf) eligible US Galaxy devices

* Pump.fun lets new tokens [pair with any coin](https://x.com/Pumpfun/status/2108265460697624755) launched on the platform

* DWF Labs affiliates sue BitGo for [$141M](https://www.chooserich.live/story/dwf-labs-sues-bitgo-ecniar4) over early token sales

* Thailand's SEC finalizes rules allowing [Bitcoin and Ether ETFs](https://www.chooserich.live/story/thailand-sec-bitcoin-ether-etf-rules-wwdgb58) to trade

* Securitize launches tokenized US stocks on Solana with [1:1 backing](https://www.chooserich.live/story/securitize-tokenized-stocks-solana-aeud3jz)

* Solana's Orca merges with Loopscale to form [Formation](https://www.chooserich.live/story/orca-loopscale-merge-formation-8biy2ex), targeting AI, robotics and defense financing

* ESMA gives EU crypto firms [three months](https://www.chooserich.live/story/esma-non-mica-stablecoins-exit-p7fufqg) to exit non-MiCA-compliant stablecoins

🧠 Crypto News Brief: Risk-off mood rules the tape: bitcoin briefly sank to a three-week low on Iran jitters, high yields and heavy ETF outflows. Meanwhile, regulators from the EU to Thailand keep reshaping crypto's rulebook. 📉 Bitcoin Slips to Three-Week Low as Iran Jitters Trigger $1B Liquidation Flush Bitcoin dropped below $81,000 to a nearly three-week low as oil climbed on Iran strike fears and elevated Treasury yields weighed on risk assets, triggering roughly $1 billion in crypto liquidations, with ether positions hit hardest. BTC has since steadied near $82,500 after President Trump ruled out an Iran strike before the U.S. midterms. Read full story ⚖️ EU Gives Crypto Platforms Three Months to Drop Non-MiCA Stablecoins The European Securities and Markets Authority has given MiCA-authorized crypto platforms three months to stop offering stablecoins that lack MiCA authorization, a group that includes Tether's USDT and PayPal's PYUSD. Platforms must block new access to these tokens, while national regulators oversee existing customer holdings. More details 💸 Bitcoin and Ether ETF Outflows Swell Toward $1B in October Bitcoin and ether ETF outflows for October are swelling toward $1 billion. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs shed about $485 million on Wednesday, their worst day since June, and another $244 million on Thursday, while XRP ETFs were the only crypto funds to post inflows. Read more 🏛️ U.S. Government Moves $1B in Seized Bitfinex Bitcoin A government-controlled wallet holding bitcoin seized from the 2016 Bitfinex hack moved 12,267 BTC, worth roughly $1 billion, in a single transaction on Thursday. The coins went to a new, unlabeled address rather than an exchange, so there is no sign of a sale yet, but traders are watching closely after other seized coins reached Coinbase Prime a day earlier. See details 🌏 Thailand Finalizes Bitcoin and Ether ETF Rules, Effective Oct. 16 Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission has finalized rules for bitcoin and ether exchange-traded funds, with the framework set to take effect on October 16. The move paves the way for regulated ETF access to the two largest cryptocurrencies in Thailand. A few years ago I arrived in Zimbabwe and found my hotel full of bankers swearing loudly. The president, Emmerson Mnangagwa, had just banned bank lending. His reasoning was a little hard to follow, for his expertise lay more in cracking heads than analysing spreads, but it went something like this. He claimed the local currency was weak, not because his spendthrift government was printing too much of it, but because speculators were borrowing to bet against it. So he choked off credit to the whole country. Happily, this insane policy lasted little more than a week. But it was a reminder of how much harm politicians can do when they fail to understand how credit works.  Which brings me to this week’s cover story, looking at the turmoil in rich-world government-bond markets. It goes without saying that rich countries are not like Zimbabwe. But some of the things rich-world politicians have been saying of late are, shall we say, on the Mnangagwa spectrum. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, France’s populist-left presidential candidate, says his country should “set fire” to a large share of its debt. Donald Trump, when not trying to intimidate governors of the Federal Reserve, has mused that inflation could reduce America’s debts “very rapidly”. A British MP recently said that if bond markets did not like the Labour government’s spending plans, they would just have to “fall in line”.  None of this reassures investors. The public debts of big advanced economies have roughly doubled, relative to GDP, since the turn of the century. Even before the latest bond sell-off, the governments of these countries were forecast to spend 8% of tax revenues on net debt interest this year. Yet many governments refuse to tighten their belts. At some point, bond-buyers will revolt.  Europe is where the danger looms largest. Its governments must compete for footloose capital with ravenous AI firms, even as the Russian menace pushes them to spend more on defence and their energy-importing economies are buffeted by costly fuel. And the risk is greatest of all in France, where protests are exploding, lawmakers struggle to agree even on tiny budget cuts, and Marine Le Pen promises that the pension age can fall as people live longer.
